name: Somatropin
lead: Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH or HGH), a biosynthetic form of the pituitary hormone whose amino acid sequence matches the natural hormone. It is prescribed to treat growth hormone deficiency in children and adults, and several other conditions involving growth failure or body-composition change, and it has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for these uses since the mid-1980s.[1][2]

In terms of appearance, somatropin acts on two things people care about: height and body composition. In children whose growth plates are still open and who have a recognised growth disorder, treatment raises growth velocity and can add adult height, for example about 5 to 8 cm in Turner syndrome in the figures cited by Wikipedia.[1][21] In adults with diagnosed deficiency, replacement tends to increase muscle mass, decrease fat mass and improve bone density and lipids.[1] These effects are the basis for its appeal in looksmaxxing and physique communities, where teenagers ask about it for height and bodybuilders discuss it alongside anabolic steroids and insulin for leanness, muscle and recovery.[16][18][27][28]

Outside approved indications the picture is different. In a 2003 pair of editorials, the New England Journal of Medicine said there was no evidence that HGH is safe and effective in healthy adults or older people, and stressed that the risks of long-term treatment were unknown.[1] A 2008 meta-analysis summarized by Wikipedia found that GH reduces body fat and increases lean body mass in healthy adults but did not show increased strength, and a Stanford meta-analysis in healthy elderly people found about 2 kg more lean mass, possibly reflecting water retention.[23][21] Chronic excess of growth hormone occurs in the disease acromegaly, which is described by enlargement of the jaw, brow, nose, hands and feet and is a recurring reference point in forum talk about facial change.[22][15]

The research base is strongest for children with deficiency, where randomized phase 3 trials have compared daily and weekly preparations, and for adults with diagnosed deficiency, where replacement improves body composition and lipids but a long-term mortality benefit has not been shown.[1][4][5] Somatropin is prescription-only and is prohibited in sport.[1][23]

paras: Growth hormone (somatotropin) is a single-chain peptide of 191 amino acids and about 22,124 daltons, made by somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary and structurally related to prolactin.[21] The hypothalamus controls its release through growth hormone-releasing hormone, which stimulates it, and somatostatin, which inhibits it. Secretion is pulsatile, the largest pulse occurs about an hour after sleep onset, and nearly half of daily output occurs in deep non-REM sleep; sleep, exercise, fasting and insulin-related signals are described as stimulators, while high blood glucose and glucocorticoids inhibit release.[21]

GH promotes growth in two ways: directly, by binding receptors on cartilage cells, and indirectly through the JAK-STAT pathway, which drives production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) mainly in the liver.[21][2] It is broadly anabolic, increasing muscle fibre size and protein synthesis, promoting fat breakdown, increasing calcium retention and bone mineralisation, raising blood glucose and free fatty acids, and inducing insulin resistance.[21] In adults with deficiency the typical pattern is more fat mass and less muscle mass.[21] Somatropin is the recombinant form given by injection; because the natural hormone has a very short half-life, administration regimens are built around once-daily or, in newer products, once-weekly injections.[2][4]

Growth hormone deficiency is the most common pituitary hormone deficiency and a main cause of short stature in children; a systematic review of nine epidemiological studies found prevalence ranging from about 1 in 1,100 to 1 in 8,600, with heterogeneous populations and diagnostic criteria.[8] Treatment replaces the missing hormone, historically by daily injection. Pediatric indications approved over time include short stature in Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, children born small for gestational age, idiopathic short stature, SHOX deficiency, Noonan syndrome and growth failure in chronic kidney disease.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports that in Turner syndrome, doses about 20 percent higher than those used in deficiency accelerate growth and give a median adult-height gain of about 5 to 8 cm, and that in chronic kidney failure treatment may narrow but not eliminate the height deficit, which can still be about 10 cm. The article also describes idiopathic short stature as a controversial indication, with Humatrope approved for it in 2003.[1] A systematic review of achondroplasia found that growth hormone, vosoritide and limb lengthening all conferred benefits for height or growth velocity, though the long-term effects of growth hormone were unclear.[3]

The Endocrine Society has recommended individualized treatment for adults diagnosed with growth hormone deficiency, with testing in people who have structural pituitary or hypothalamic disease, surgery, irradiation or head trauma, and stringent criteria for the rare diagnosis of idiopathic deficiency in adults.[1][10] Replacement in deficient adults can improve bone density, muscle mass, fat mass and blood lipids, though a long-term mortality benefit has not been demonstrated.[1] US approvals also cover AIDS-associated wasting and short bowel syndrome in adults.[1][2]

Height is the appearance outcome most directly tied to growth hormone, and it is the basis of looksmax.org threads in which teenage users ask whether HGH at ages as young as 14 to 16 is worth it for height.[27][28] Published trials of height gain concern children with a diagnosed disorder: weekly and daily products have been compared in deficiency, and registered trials cover idiopathic short stature, children born small for gestational age and other indications.[4][5][13][14] Growth hormone acts on cartilage growth plates, so its height effect depends on plates that remain open; excess GH after plates close does not lengthen bones but causes thickening of bone and soft tissue, as in acromegaly.[22][21]

In deficient adults, replacement lowers fat and raises muscle mass.[1] In healthy adults, a 2008 meta-analysis summarized by Wikipedia found reduced body fat and increased lean body mass but not strength, and its authors concluded that claims of enhanced physical performance were not supported by the literature; the Stanford elderly meta-analysis found about 2 kg more lean mass and about 2 kg less fat, with no strength improvement.[23][21] Some of the lean-mass gain may be water retention.[21]

Chronic GH excess after growth-plate fusion causes overgrowth that usually affects the hands and feet first, followed by the forehead, jaw and nose; the lower jaw can protrude, the upper jaw widen and the teeth space apart.[22] Roughly 98 percent of acromegaly cases come from a benign pituitary adenoma, and the condition is treated by surgery, somatostatin analogues and other drugs.[22] Excess GH before the plates close causes pituitary gigantism, whose examples include Robert Wadlow, who stood 2.72 m tall.[24] Forum discussions of the 'steroid jawline' and of a physique that looks bigger sometimes invoke HGH as a cause, which is why this section appears here; no trial has tested somatropin for cosmetic facial change in healthy people.[15][18]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: In physique and gear communities, HGH is discussed as an add-on to anabolic steroids and insulin for muscle, leanness and recovery, and some members describe it as a route to faces and physiques that appear 'bigger'; one T Nation commenter attributes a 'phenomenal response' to anabolic steroids and HGH with insulin.[18][15] Members of the same forum describe buying it through gray-market channels, and arguments about whether a particular physique reflects HGH use recur in long threads.[17][15] A 2026 forum post quotes news coverage describing looksmaxxers among those using performance-enhancing drugs, including human growth hormone.[16]

On looksmax.org, HGH has its own cluster of threads with titles such as 'hgh at 14', 'hgh at 15' and 'hgh at 16 for height is it worth it', in which teenagers ask about its effects on height, alongside threads on sourcing, product strains and experiences.[27][28] An opening post in one thread presents a list of purported benefits including bone health, height, muscle, anti-ageing and energy, and a reply in the thread mocks it as machine-written text.[30] A long community 'megaguide' compares recombinant brands such as Genotropin, Norditropin and Jintropin and states that all lab-made HGH is recombinant, with different strains differing in characteristics; a reply notes that 'it's all somatropin at the end of the day'.[29] These threads are presented here as a record of community discussion, not as guidance.

Beyond the forums, HGH is associated with high-profile wellness culture: a 2014 Hacker News thread discusses a Bloomberg video in which Peter Thiel says he takes HGH, with top comments citing a Stanford report that no data show benefit for healthy people and raising risks, while a 2019 headline posted there reports new guidelines advising against growth hormone for anti-ageing.[25][26]
Most published human trials of somatropin concern children and adults with a recognized medical indication rather than healthy people seeking cosmetic effects.

Pediatric growth hormone deficiency: A 12-month phase 3 trial of 228 prepubertal children compared weekly somatrogon with daily somatropin and found annualized height velocity of 10.10 cm per year versus 9.78 cm per year, meeting the non-inferiority margin.[4] A 52-week phase 3 trial (heiGHt) of 161 treatment-naive children found weekly lonapegsomatropin gave annualized height velocity of 11.2 cm per year versus 10.3 cm per year for daily somatropin.[5] The REAL4 trial of weekly somapacitan in children with deficiency has reported efficacy and tolerability at one year and results at three years.[6][19] A phase 3 trial has also tested somapacitan in children born small for gestational age.[7]

Registered trials: ClinicalTrials.gov lists studies of Genotropin in children with intrauterine growth retardation, Saizen in idiopathic short stature, Omnitrope in short children born small for gestational age, Norditropin in adults with Prader-Willi syndrome, and Serostim in HIV-associated adipose redistribution syndrome.[11][12][13][14]

Metabolism: A randomized trial showed that growth hormone-induced lipolysis and insulin resistance could be abrogated by a ketone body infusion, illustrating the hormone's effects on fat breakdown and glucose handling.[20]

Healthy adults: Wikipedia summarises that there is no evidence that HGH use in healthy adults or older people is safe and effective, and that a small controlled study in critically ill intensive care patients found higher mortality in those given GH.[1] A 2008 meta-analysis summarized on Wikipedia found reduced fat and increased lean mass but no strength gain and possible reduced exercise capacity.[23] No published trial has tested somatropin for cosmetic facial or body outcomes in healthy people.

Growth hormone treatment usually decreases insulin sensitivity, although some studies of GH-treated adults with hypopituitarism found no increase in diabetes incidence.[1] Earlier concern that GH raised cancer risk was examined in a large study of 6,840 adults treated with GH, which found no overall increase in primary cancer risk over relatively short follow-up, with elevated rates in subgroups defined by age under 35 or childhood-onset deficiency.[1] In August 2011 the FDA issued a safety communication saying evidence on recombinant GH and increased risk of death was inconclusive.[1]

Side effects of non-medical use listed in the sports literature include swollen hands and feet, joint pain, fluid retention and excessive sweating.[23] Chronic excess of growth hormone, as in acromegaly, is clinically associated with enlargement of the jaw, brow, hands and feet, carpal tunnel syndrome, insulin resistance and heart and metabolic complications; untreated, life expectancy is reduced by about 10 years.[1][22] Cadaver-derived growth hormone was linked to Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease before it was withdrawn in 1985.[1][2]

Somatropin binds growth hormone receptors and activates JAK2/STAT signalling, which prompts the liver and other tissues to produce insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and promotes linear bone growth, increases muscle and bone mass, reduces fat mass and influences protein, carbohydrate, lipid and mineral metabolism.[2] It is given by subcutaneous injection, usually once daily; long-acting once-weekly products (lonapegsomatropin, somapacitan, somatrogon) have been tested against daily somatropin in children.[4][5][6] Somapacitan (Sogroya) was approved in the US in August 2020 as the first once-weekly hGH therapy.[1]

By the mid-twentieth century endocrinologists understood the features of growth hormone deficiency, but pig and cow hormone did not work in humans because of species differences. Charles Stratton, exhibited by P. T. Barnum as General Tom Thumb, is cited by Wikipedia as the best-known example of untreated congenital GH deficiency.[1] In the late 1950s Maurice Raben purified enough GH from human pituitary glands to treat a deficient boy, and in 1960 the US National Pituitary Agency was formed to collect glands and distribute the hormone for research protocols; other countries set up similar agencies. From 1963 to 1985 about 7,700 children in the US and 27,000 worldwide received cadaver-derived GH.[1][9]

In 1981 Genentech, collaborating with Kabi, developed recombinant human GH using recombinant DNA technology. In 1985 four young adults who had received pituitary GH in the 1960s developed Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and use of human pituitary GH rapidly ceased; between 1985 and 2003 there were 26 such cases among recipients of pre-1977 hormone. Genentech's recombinant product, Protropin (methionyl-GH, or somatrem), was approved the same year, with initial treatment costs of US$10,000 to $30,000 per year.[1][2] Subsequent FDA approvals extended indications to chronic kidney disease (1993), adult deficiency (1996), Turner syndrome (1997), Prader-Willi syndrome (2000), small for gestational age (2001), idiopathic short stature (2003), SHOX deficiency (2006) and Noonan syndrome (2007), according to one summary.[2] Lonapegsomatropin was approved in the US in August 2021.[1]

Daniel Rudman's 1990 study of men over 60 drew wide attention to growth hormone as a rejuvenating agent, and Ronald Klatz's 1997 book promoted it as an anti-ageing treatment; the internet later produced many supplements marketed as HGH boosters, which prompted the 2003 New England Journal of Medicine editorials.[1] The Stanford meta-analysis in elderly adults found lean mass rose and fat fell but strength did not improve.[21]

Wikipedia dates the first described doping use of GH to Dan Duchaine's 1982 Underground Steroid Handbook, just after recombinant hormone became available in 1981.[21][23] The International Olympic Committee banned HGH in 1989, and blood tests able to distinguish natural from recombinant GH led to enforcement in the early 2000s, with the 2004 Athens Olympics using such tests.[23][21] Urine tests could not detect GH doping.[21] The same Wikipedia article says recombinant GH is hard to detect because it closely matches the body's own hormone, and describes use in power sports, bodybuilding, swimming and cycling, often with steroids, testosterone or EPO.[23] The hormone's extra-medical use has been a controversy for about fifty years; Wikipedia notes that a rhesus-monkey form featured in the lore of the underground steroid community, with fraudulent versions reportedly sold in gyms.[1]

Somatropin is a prescription medicine in the United States and many other countries; the FDA has not approved it for performance enhancement, and distributing or using it without a prescription is described as illegal.[21][23] It is prohibited by the IOC, NCAA and other athletic bodies.[21]

lore.intro: On T Nation and looksmax.org, HGH is discussed as a premium addition to steroid regimens, as a presumed cause of particular facial or body appearance, as a height option for teenagers, and as an expensive, hard-to-source product.[15][17][18][27][28]

claims.claim: HGH use adds to a 'steroid look' and contributes to jaw and facial width
claims.believers: Posters in long T Nation threads argue about whether a physique lacks the 'steroid jawline' only because the person did not use growth hormone, and another thread attributes a 'phenomenal response' to steroids and HGH with insulin.[15][18]
claims.experts: Chronic GH excess in acromegaly produces enlargement of the jaw, brow and nose after growth plates close, and the condition carries heart and metabolic complications; no trial has tested GH as a cosmetic facial treatment in healthy adults.[22][1]

claims.claim: HGH is a safe anti-ageing and muscle-building therapy for healthy adults
claims.believers: Forum members describe HGH as part of recovery and joint-health routines and discuss obtaining it through informal channels.[17][15]
claims.experts: The New England Journal of Medicine editorials of 2003 stated there is no evidence of safety and efficacy in healthy adults or the elderly; a 2008 meta-analysis found fat loss and lean-mass gain without strength gain, and benefits documented in deficient adults include body-composition and lipid changes without proven mortality benefit.[1][23]

claims.claim: Teenagers can use HGH to add height
claims.believers: Looksmax.org threads titled around taking HGH at 14, 15 or 16 for height show teenagers asking whether it is worth it.[27][28]
claims.experts: Controlled trials show added growth velocity and adult height in children with diagnosed deficiency, Turner syndrome and some other conditions; the idiopathic short stature indication has been described as controversial, and no published trial has tested it in healthy teenagers of typical height.[1][4][5]

claims.claim: GH combined with insulin and anabolic steroids is an especially effective stack
claims.believers: A T Nation commenter describes a 'phenomenal response' to anabolic steroids and HGH with insulin in the context of discussing physique width.[18]
claims.experts: Published sources describe GH as typically decreasing insulin sensitivity and show lipolysis and insulin resistance as linked effects; no study has tested the combination for appearance.[1][20]

claims.claim: Different HGH 'strains' and brands differ meaningfully
claims.believers: A looksmax.org megaguide compares recombinant brands and argues strains differ in production and characteristics.[29]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and regulators describe somatropin as recombinant human GH whose amino acid sequence is identical to the natural hormone; a reply in the thread itself says it is all somatropin.[1][29]

claims.claim: Gray-market HGH is available at stable prices and is genuine
claims.believers: A T Nation member reports ordering HGH and finding prices unchanged.[17]
claims.experts: Wikipedia records that a counterfeit rhesus-GH product circulated in gyms in the steroid underground; GH is a prescription-only drug and prohibited in sport.[1][23]
